`insertAdjacentHTML` is only broken in the sense of its specification, which on its own is not a good reason of course. https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10122 discusses some reasons for why we might want a replacement. Yea it's "splice" rather than "insert", which is perhaps more verbose but is a common lower level primitive for mutations?

It's quite easy to implement the #10122 semantics on top of the proposal here, while keeping the consistency with passing the rest of the options (sanitizer, streaming, allow-scripts), or add them as sugar into the platform (e.g. `position` instead of `before` and `after`).

... the other option for `insertAdjacentHTML` is to have `insertHTML` and `insertHTMLUnsafe` methods (so 6 instead of 4) that have the `position` argument instead of `before` + `after` and doesn't remove any element... but then if we want to add streaming to that we end up with 8 methods altogether which starts to feel like a lot? 

4 HTML-setting methods with splicing feels like a good balance to me with leaving it open to adding `insert*` variants in the future.

Over in WordPress we’ve been stewing on this issue for some time now, ever since we built a pure-PHP HTML5 parser. We are wanting to provide a convenient API for server-side code to understand and manipulate HTML, ideally to do things like stitch in HTML fragments from one document into another. For us, this means we are fundamentally less concerned with script execution and more concerned with escaping outside of the context in which an edit is made. For instance, when inserting into the DOM it’s impossible to escape from the parent. It’s possible to construct invalid DOM trees which cannot be re-serialized into HTML. One example of this is creating a `P` element as a child inside of another `P` element. But in the HTML world we have this conundrum where if we allow the insertion of such a `

` inside another open `P` element, we have allowed server-side code to create HTML which will parse differently once it reaches the browsers. This is why this issue has been delayed and held up for so long for us, because the fragment parsing algorithm isn’t relevant for this case, but it seems like the issue at hand with streaming HTML _is_ identical or close enough to be relevant. The fundamental question I would love to see specified and standardized is what happens when something appears which should breach a context. Maybe here it’s still left to the DOM and unrepresentable DOM trees are the answer, but I see three possible ways to handle this on the server: - Outright reject updates which would cause any open element to close, if that open element is a parent or ancestor of the node in which inner HTML was set or changed. - Remove elements which would trigger modifications to the open elements. This could lead to extreme behavior in edge cases and distorts updates. - Wrap the offending elements and reconstruct them via DOM operations once the page loads. E.g. if setting inner HTML to `

` when already inside an `H1` element, wrap it as ``. This is pretty relevant for any system that brings together separate HTML snippets or templates, and I would imagine even those which heavily modify the page via JS. It’s nice that the DOM allows for unrepresentable constructions, but it would be ideal to be able to agree on the server and the client on what the rendered HTML will do. Some API which provides for a kind of isolation of a parent element for inner markup changes would be extremely helpful. _“No matter what HTML is set to the inside of this element, it will not bleed into the surrounding page.”_ This is helpful for proper understanding, it’s helpful for security issues, and it’s helpful for the resilience of sites which deal with user-supplied content.

` In our experimentation we have found cases where the missing elements on the stack of open elements is relevant for tokens which impact the insertion mode, affect integration points and name spacing, and a number of other state values. In WordPress/wordpress-develop#7777 we started looking at ways to extend the fragment parser to clone the stack of open elements and provide guards which would detect if the parsing algorithm attempted to close any open element. I have explored a weaker approach in [a builder class](https://gist.github.com/dmsnell/ff758c13e8d41bf9f0b75f3fd42ad1e5#file-html_serialization_builder-php-L64-L100) which simply examines whether there are any remaining tokens in the new inner HTML after the outer-most stack is back to the depth it had when the parsing started. In all of the work I’ve explored, the one simple rule that I _think_ is relevant to isolate changes is to somehow freeze the stack of open elements, run the parse algorithm in place, and if there are changes or pops to the stack of open elements above the point of setting inner HTML, it’s a violation. Probably other things need to be examined as well, such as whether the parse changed the insertion mode, updated the form pointer, changed the document encoding, etc… --- Thanks for asking. I hope this clarifies things instead of making them less clear. The entire problem remains that the DOM operations allow creating DOM trees which cannot be represented in HTML. Even the latest work to bring in `DOM\HtmlDocument` in PHP leave us without reasonable tools to mix and match HTML from different sources because updates through its internal DOM don’t round-trip (we can’t send it’s internal DOM to a browser to we have to serialize, which creates these situations where the browser reads a different DOM than we had on the server). It seems like streaming into the DOM via HTML is going to present similar quandaries. Suppose we load in the HTML for a comment on a blog. Should that comment be allowed to interrupt the flow of the page? How can we ensure that it remains isolated and inert?

In terms of API design, I think it would help to summarize what variables we have, and which ones only apply based on others.

Am I missing any variables? Are any of these variables out of scope for what we're doing here?

In terms of the multiple methods vs options debate, some thoughts:
- Different methods are generally better when the return types are different, or when vastly different overloads are desired. 
- Different methods work better when the use cases are significantly different
- Options are more extensible: far easier to add a new option, than a new set of methods
- The more the variables, the more the pendulum swings towards options, because:
	- With many variables, you end up getting combinatorial explosion if you try to encode the parameters in method names
	- Options are generally more discoverable than method names, as people look up the docs of the method they're using anyway, but not necessarily docs for adjacent methods
	- With more than one variable, it often becomes hard to remember the order in which parameters are encoded in the method name 
	- Options work better when variables may be set dynamically (dynamic method names are possible, but more awkward)
- Different methods work well when you want to allow an arbitrary number of arguments (like in `element.append()`) which precludes using an options bag. However, in many cases, the need to parameterize further via options comes up later, so I think designing an API that can accommodate an options bag (even if the MVP doesn't include it) tends to be a safer bet. The arbitrary number of arguments can often be accommodated via an iterable (e.g. an array of nodes).

Just to reiterate what I said about script running at TPAC:

Take:

```html
<script>
  document.currentScript.parentElement.append('\nhello from inline script');
</script>
<script src="script-1.js"></script>
<script src="script-2.js"></script>
```

And assume each script is:

```js
document.currentScript.parentElement.append('\nhello from script-(n)');
```

The HTML parser will produce:

```html
<script>…</script>
hello from inline script
<script src="script-1.js"></script>
hello from script-1
<script src="script-2.js"></script>
hello from script-2
```

I think it's important for `streamHTMLUnsafe({ runScripts: true })` to produce the same result.

Right now, `createContextualFragment` will produce:

```html
<script>…</script>
<script src="script-1.js"></script>
<script src="script-2.js"></script>
hello from inline script
hello from script-2
hello from script-1
```

…where the order of script-2 and script-1 is racy.

While refactoring [HTML fragment parsing algorithm](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#html-fragment-parsing-algorithm) to support `streamHTMLUnsafe()` a few issues have surfaced that I'd like to document here for discussion. ## Inert document vs. document fragment The spec uses an inert document as the parser document, and first inserts nodes into that document. The `innerHTML` setter then moves the nodes to a `DocumentFragment`, and finally uses [replace all](https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-node-replace-all) to finish the job. No implementations seem to use an inert document, and there are observable side effects of this. @noamr has tested `new Range().createContextualFragment('')` and this fetches the image in all browsers, which wouldn't happen if an inert document was used. My thinking is now to align the spec with implementations, so that the parser document is the main document and the fragment parser adds nodes to a `DocumentFragment`. ## `streamHTMLUnsafe()` insertion point If we do the above, a natural next step is to make the insertion point a parser argument/setting, so that the fragment parser can insert either into `DocumentFragment` or directly into an element in the document in the case of `streamHTMLUnsafe()`. ## `runScripts` details Supporting `runScripts` for `setHTMLUnsafe()` and `streamHTMLUnsafe()` raises the question of parser-blocking scripts, i.e. when `

I think it's ok for `setHTMLUnsafe()` and `streamHTMLUnsafe()` to be different in this case. I can't see a way to do it like the main parser but be synchronous. In fact, I thought that was one of the reasons why things like `innerHTML` have this divergent behaviour.

It'd be nice if `setHTMLUnsafe()` still resulted in scripts executing in the 'right' order, but I can't see how it can 'block' the parser.

Perhaps `setHTMLUnsafe()` could have an option that resulted in it being async, as in returning a promise?

I agree, `setHTMLUnsafe()` can't behave like the main parser in this regard while being sync.

In order to minimize differences, however, I wonder if the default for both `setHTMLUnsafe()` and `streamHTMLUnsafe()` should be non-parser-blocking, and that `streamHTMLUnsafe()` could opt in to it to be more like the main parser?

I think letting `setHTMLUnsafe()` return a promise, especially based on a parameter, is perhaps giving a bit too much space in a new API to an old behavior that we regret in the platform. If it can be done by `streamHTMLUnsafe()` with an opt-in, then wrapping that in a helper that takes a single string and returns a promise would be trivial.

I've created this comprehensive table to explain how the different modes of HTML, including existing ones, affect script execution as well as observable behavior such as image preloading upon creation.

| Method | Classic scripts? | Async scripts? | Defer/module scripts? | Should images preload? | Insert into | Script state |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :---  | :--- |
| `<template>` | * | * | * | No | Target | Enabled |
| `createContextualFragment` | After | After | After | Yes | Fragment | Enabled |
| `streamHTML` | No | No | No | No | Inert | Disabled |
| `setHTML` | No | No | No | No | Fragment | Disabled |
| `innerHTML setter` | No | No | No | N/A | Fragment | Disabled |
| `setHTMLUnsafe()` | No | No | No | N/A  | Fragment | Disabled |
| `setHTMLUnsafe({sanitizer})` | No | No | No | No | Fragment | Disabled |
| `setHTMLUnsafe({sanitizer, runScripts})` | After | After | After | No | Fragment | Enabled |
| `setHTMLUnsafe({runScripts})` | After | After | After | N/A | Fragment | Enabled |
| `streamHTMLUnsafe({runScripts})` | Block parsing | Fetch async | At end of stream | N/A | Target | Enabled |
| `streamHTMLUnsafe({sanitizer, runScripts})` | Block parsing | Fetch async | At end of stream | No | Target | Enabled |
| `streamHTMLUnsafe()` | No | No | No | N/A | Target | Disabled |
| `streamHTMLUnsafe(sanitizer)` | No | No | No | No | Target | Disabled |

Some take aways from the above as to how this can be spec'ed/implemented:
- Sanitizer+template requires a creation-time document, to avoid the image preloading side effect.
   `createContextualFragment` requires not having one. Other modes are agnostic.
- An intermediate fragment is needed for all set* methods
- Whether scripts are disabled should be propagated to script creation, rather rely on current implicit behavior based on the inert document
- `streamHTMLUnsafe` + `runScripts`: this needs some special handling of `defer`, to defer executing the scripts until the stream is closed.

I've summarized a lot of the thinking here, as well as how this ties to the sanitizer and trusted types, to an [explainer](https://github.com/WICG/declarative-partial-updates/blob/main/dynamic-markup-revamped-explainer.md).

A note regarding `createContextualFragment`: I've researched this further and the current behavior is spec-compliant after all, because images are also loaded when adopted. So when an image is created in the inert document and then adopted to the contextual `DocumentFragment`, and will start fetching the resource on *adoption* rather than on *creation*. 

This makes the whole issue around the creation document unobsrevable.

Even though the spec currently says to create a document fragment and to then insert it for the `innerHTML` setter, Gecko parses directly into the context node. It would be bad if doing things the safer way made things slower.

If we're going to do `streamHTMLUnsafe(sanitizer)` anyway, then we are going to need a sanitizer that runs as part of tree construction instead of running as a post processing step on a constructed inert tree.

Therefore, it will probably makes sense to implement `setHTMLUnsafe({sanitizer})` eventually by parsing directly into the context node with the sanitizer mechanism that will be created for `streamHTMLUnsafe(sanitizer)`. It would be bad for the spec to constrain things in a way that would make this infeasible.

One potential source of difference is the [Blink-compatible insertion depth limit](https://searchfox.org/firefox-main/rev/72a543fee7d16f07f6f04bd6caf7c7692ed291bf/parser/html/nsHtml5TreeBuilder.cpp#4750-4757), which I don't see in the actual spec by searching for 510, 511, or 512. If some items wouldn't end up on the tree builder stack with `streamHTMLUnsafe(sanitizer)` but did with `setHTMLUnsafe({sanitizer})`, that would be a source of differences. The Blink-compatible insertion depth limit is already a bit silly in fragment parsing, since it doesn't adapt to what depth the context node is at, so with fragment parsing (as with tree manipulation by `appendChild`) it's still possible for layout to exhaust the stack of the thread that layout runs on.

@noamr is it in scope of this work to also handle client-side backpressure when streaming HTML? The current problem with client-side streaming and by extension `document.write` is that HTML chunks could arrive in a very different shape:

1. Lots of tiny HTML chunks in quick succession
2. Few very large HTML chunks with some delay in between

These both impose a problem of client-side rendering performance. Writing too many chunks could introduce jank and triggering full render cycle way too frequently. Writing massive chunks could halt the page for seconds.

Right now we're dealing with that by having a custom rendering balancer that has a fixed time window to collect chunks, join them and then split into consumable size. It would be really convenient if Web Platform could provide a similar mechanism that would be deeply integrated with browser internals to achieve best possible performance regardless of network conditions and server capacity.

----

I've also identified that `document.write` does not work with Web Components in Safari. We have to patch the element's prototype and manually trigger lifecycle in order for them to work. I would appreciate if Web Platform also had tests for this integration.

@CyberAP Unlike `document.write()`, the streaming APIs here rely on web streams, which support backpressure tweaking as part of the streams spec. You can achieve this kind of chunk balancing by piping an input stream through a `TransformStream` that optimizes the kind of edge cases you're mentioning, before reaching the HTML parser's input stream.

In addition, if this ends up being insufficient, the options dictionary passed to the streaming API is structured in a way that can be extended in the future to support additional arguments, e.g. `element.streamHTML({runScripts: true, chunkStrategy: "smooth"})` or some such; However it's beyond the scope of this initial set of features (we have to start somewhere!)
